extracted.subtask_description: Apply Grunig's situational theory to measure and classify organizational publics using three independent variables (problem recognition, constraint recognition, level of involvement), two communication behavior variables (information seeking and processing), and resultant communication effects to guide PR strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Variable #1—Problem Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem recognition: people do not think or communicate about an issue unless they perceive that something needs to be done to improve the situation; when they detect a problem they enter the behavioral molecule and are more likely to communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem recognition increases likelihood of both information seeking and processing and of communication effects. Measure by asking respondents how often they 'stop to think' about specified issues (often, sometimes, rarely, never). Use this per organizational consequence/issue (see Exhibit 7-1). High problem recognition helps identify members of publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Variable A—Information Seeking (Active Communication Behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information seeking: active communication behavior in which members look for information and try to understand it; such publics become aware and often active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively communicating publics process information more effectively and messages aimed at them tend to be more effective. Grunig measured seeking by asking likelihood of sending for a hypothetical free brochure on an issue. Use seeking probabilities to predict effectiveness of informational outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Variable B—Information Processing (Passive Communication Behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information processing: passive communication behavior in which members do not seek information but may process information that reaches them randomly (without effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processed information has fewer effects than sought information; processed audiences require different message strategies (style/creative devices) to attract attention. Grunig measured processing by asking how much attention respondents would pay to a hypothetical TV news opening line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Variable #2—Constraint Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraint recognition: the extent to which people perceive obstacles or constraints in a situation that limit their freedom to plan or act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High constraint recognition reduces likelihood of information seeking and processing because information has less value when people feel they cannot act. Measure by asking whether a person's efforts would make 'a great deal/some/very little/no difference' for each issue (Exhibit 7-1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Variable #3—Level of Involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of involvement: the extent to which people connect themselves personally to the situation (perceive the issue affects or could affect them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High involvement tends to increase problem recognition and decrease constraint recognition, making active seeking more likely. Measure by asking respondents the strength of their personal connection to each issue (strong, moderate, weak, none). High involvement distinguishes active vs. passive communication behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement procedures for the three variables (Exhibit 7-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational measurement: measure problem recognition, constraint recognition, and level of involvement separately for each organizational consequence/issue; typically with single survey items per variable per issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example survey items: (1) Problem recognition — 'How often do you stop to think about [issue]? (often/sometimes/rarely/never)'; (2) Constraint recognition — 'Would your efforts make a great deal/some/very little/no difference?'; (3) Level of involvement — 'To what extent do you see a connection between yourself and this situation? (strong/moderate/weak/none)'. Use telephone for few issues, mail questionnaires for many (up to ~16 issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining publics via combinations of the three variables (eight publics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment publics by dichotomizing each variable (high/low) to produce eight combinations (2x2x2) corresponding to behavior types and public categories (e.g., problem-facing, constrained behavior, routine behavior, fatalistic behavior, each with high- or low-involvement variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the eight-category typology (e.g., HIPF = high-involvement problem-facing) to infer likely communication behaviors (seeking/processing) and public status (active, aware, latent, nonpublic). Table 7-1 links combinations to expected public types and behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication effects metrics (message retention, cognition, attitude, behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication effects are dependent outcomes beyond seeking/processing: message retention (recall of factual message content), cognitions (development of pro- or anti-issue beliefs), attitudes (evaluative judgments), and behavior (actions taken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure message retention with factual multiple-choice items; measure cognitions via pro-/antibusiness cognitive items (hedge/wedge measures); measure attitude via agree/disagree on policy statements; measure behavior via self-report of actions (writing letters, boycotting, attending rallies). Use probabilities of these effects (derived empirically) to predict impact of PR messages on different publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probabilities to estimate communication likelihood and resource allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute probabilities of information seeking, processing, and communication effects for each type of public to predict the relative frequency (probability) of outcomes and to help decide whether to invest in communication with that public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grunig's empirical study produced probabilities (e.g., total probability seeking 40%, processing 79%) and per-public probabilities (Table 7-2). Use these probabilities to estimate cost-effectiveness: do not expend resources on publics with low probabilities unless the consequence is severe or you can use processing to stimulate problem recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy implication #1 — Avoid low-probability publics
rubrics_metrics.description: If a public has low probability of information seeking/processing and low probability that directed messages will be effective, generally avoid investing PR resources to reach that public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the public is linked via an enabling/critical consequence (high potential harm), consider alternate approaches; otherwise resource allocation should favor publics with higher probabilities of communication effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy implication #2 — Use processing-oriented messaging to spark problem recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: For publics that will not seek information but may process it, design messages to be processed randomly; partial message retention can stimulate problem recognition and lead publics to seek more information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that messages may produce only partial retention but can still shift a public from low-probability to higher-probability of seeking/processing. Use channels where incidental exposure occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy implication #3 — Use style/creativity for passive (processing) publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Passively communicating publics require stylistic and creative devices to attract attention and lure them into processing information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use photos, illustrations, clever writing, catchy phrases, slogans, and other attention-getting devices in messages targeted at processing publics (examples: memorable slogans, striking visuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy implication #4 — Maintain high profile with active publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Active publics (high seeking/behavior probabilities) must be actively engaged by the organization because if the organization does not communicate, these publics will seek information elsewhere and may form unfavorable cognitions/attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not maintain a low public profile when active publics exist; proactively provide information and engage these publics since they will seek multiple sources and are difficult to persuade if neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy implication #5 — Focus on high-involvement/problem-facing publics for attitude/behavior change
rubrics_metrics.description: If the objective is to change attitudes or behavior, concentrate efforts on publics with the highest probability of change—typically high-involvement, problem-facing publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active publics seek information from many sources and are hard to persuade; however they are the most likely to develop reasoned cognitions, attitudes, and to act. For goals like fundraising, target HIPF segments for best probability of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for interactions among the three independent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: The three independent variables influence one another: level of involvement generally increases problem recognition and decreases constraint recognition, which in turn affects the distribution and frequency of the eight public types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect some public types (e.g., HIPF, LIFB) to be more common than others based on these interactions. Use this knowledge when interpreting survey scores and when prioritizing publics for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation and interpretation of probabilities (Table 7-2 findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empirical findings (Grunig's studies) to validate predicted probabilities of seeking, processing, cognition, attitude, retention, and behavior across the eight public types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret table: differences between publics are larger for seeking than processing; overall processing occurs about twice as often as seeking; message retention is relatively low compared to cognition/attitude; only a minority engage in behavior (~20%). Use these empirical patterns when setting realistic PR objectives.
